purpose: Execute the remaining267 fixed-target cases on the same engine as completed201, without duplicate201 execution. This is a common historical-source baseline, not a current-main pass count.
reused201_qualification: 197 unchanged originals and four separately corrected explicit-React protocols; retain original/corrected associations.

cases.title: A measured joule becomes warm water
cases.original_physical_forecast: 10 kJ into 100 g water should raise temperature roughly 24 K, without mass loss below boiling.

cases.title: Undo a thermal pulse
cases.original_physical_forecast: Heating then removing the same 10 kJ should return 100 g water close to its initial temperature and mass.

cases.title: Mix unequal hot and cold portions
cases.original_physical_forecast: 75 g at 20 C plus 25 g at 80 C should equilibrate near 35 C; mass should be 100 g.

cases.title: A double dose is not a double temperature rise
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal 10 kJ pulses into 100 g and 200 g water should produce approximately 2:1 temperature rises.

cases.title: Latent heat intercepts the cooling pulse
cases.original_physical_forecast: Removing 20 kJ from 100 g water initially at 5 C should give an ice/water mixture near 0 C, not liquid at -43 C.

cases.title: Boiling spends energy on disappearing liquid
cases.original_physical_forecast: 40 kJ into 100 g water at 95 C should approach 100 C and evaporate roughly 17 g rather than heat all liquid to 190 C.

cases.title: Heat dilution cannot invent energy
cases.original_physical_forecast: Mixing two equal water portions at 60 C should keep them near 60 C, not reset the second dose to room temperature.

cases.title: A tenfold acid dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Diluting 0.001 mol HCl in 100 mL water with another 900 mL should raise pH by about one unit (roughly 2 to 3).

cases.title: Acid/base cancellation and overshoot
cases.original_physical_forecast: 0.001 mol HCl followed by equal NaOH should reach near-neutral pH; another 0.001 mol NaOH should make it alkaline.

cases.title: Weak acid versus strong acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal 0.001 mol doses in 100 mL should give acetic acid a higher pH than HCl, by at least one unit.

cases.title: Half-neutralisation exposes a pKa
cases.original_physical_forecast: 0.01 mol acetic acid and 0.005 mol NaOH in 100 mL should form a buffer around pH 4.5-5.0.

cases.title: A buffer survives a small acid pulse
cases.original_physical_forecast: A half-neutralised acetate buffer should change pH far less than plain water after the same 0.0001 mol HCl pulse.

cases.title: Neutral salt is an ionic conductor
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding 0.001 mol NaCl to 100 mL water should increase conductivity substantially while leaving pH approximately neutral.

cases.title: Common ions make a silver cloud
cases.original_physical_forecast: 0.001 mol each of NaCl and AgNO3 in 100 mL should produce close to 0.001 mol solid AgCl, with conserved silver and chloride.

cases.title: Precipitation cannot depend on bottle order
cases.original_physical_forecast: Reversing the equal silver/chloride additions should leave essentially equal AgCl solid amounts and pH in the two vessels.

cases.title: Remove the cloud without removing the salt water
cases.original_physical_forecast: Filtering an AgCl suspension should retain its solid in v1 and move aqueous material to v2; total inventory should be conserved.

cases.title: Barium and sulfate meet
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal 0.001 mol BaCl2 and Na2SO4 in 100 mL should form very insoluble BaSO4, or explicitly identify unavailable chemistry.

cases.title: Chalk dissolves in acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: 0.001 mol CaCO3 should be consumed by 0.003 mol HCl in 100 mL; carbon dioxide should be accounted for and excess acid remain.

cases.title: Finite solvent leaves salt behind
cases.original_physical_forecast: 100 g NaCl in 100 g water should leave substantial undissolved solid instead of an unlimited solution.

cases.title: Extra solvent rescues leftover salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding another 500 mL water to 50 g NaCl in 100 g water should dissolve the residual solid.

cases.title: Drying a dilute salt solution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Evaporating 90% of the solvent from 0.001 mol NaCl in 100 g water should conserve sodium/chloride while increasing concentration roughly tenfold.

cases.title: A quarter of a solution carries a quarter of its salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: Decanting fraction 0.25 should send about 25% of dissolved NaCl and water to v2 and conserve combined mass.

cases.title: Splitting and reuniting a solution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Decant 0.4 into v2 then all of v2 back to v1 should restore initial inventory, temperature, and pH within numerical tolerance.

cases.title: A small sealed headspace makes fizz push back
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acidifying 0.001 mol NaHCO3 with 0.002 mol HCl over a sealed 10 mL headspace should raise pressure above ambient and retain carbon.

cases.title: Headspace size controls pressure
cases.original_physical_forecast: The same acid/carbonate doses should produce higher final pressure over 10 mL than 100 mL sealed headspace.

cases.title: Uncorking releases the compressed gas
cases.original_physical_forecast: Opening an acid/carbonate vessel should restore ambient gas pressure and account for vented gas without losing sodium/chloride.

cases.title: Fixed pressure trades pressure rise for expansion
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid/carbonate under 1 bar regulation should stay near 1 bar and increase gas volume or explicitly state the unsupported constraint.

cases.title: Sweeping carbon dioxide out
cases.original_physical_forecast: A nitrogen sweep after a finite CO2 dose should lower retained carbon and raise pH relative to the carbonated state, with a gas-transfer account.

cases.title: A sacrificial zinc strip plates copper
cases.original_physical_forecast: Zinc in 0.001 mol CuSO4 solution should produce copper metal and consume zinc; mass/inventory should show the exchange.

cases.title: Copper refuses the reverse displacement
cases.original_physical_forecast: Copper in ZnSO4 should not plate zinc; an explicit no-reaction result should be chemically distinguished from missing chemistry.

cases.title: A concentration cell vanishes at equality
cases.original_physical_forecast: Identical copper half-cells should give near-zero voltage; diluting one tenfold should produce a nonzero voltage of order tens of mV.

cases.title: Purple colour follows concentration
cases.original_physical_forecast: Tenfold dilution of dilute KMnO4 should reduce absorbance and fade purple toward pink without losing permanganate inventory.

cases.title: A salt flame is not fuel
cases.original_physical_forecast: Igniting NaCl should report a yellow sodium flame signature or a boundary, without consuming salt as combustible fuel.

cases.title: Magnesium gains oxygen mass
cases.original_physical_forecast: Igniting 0.001 mol Mg should create MgO and gain about 0.016 g from atmospheric oxygen, with the external mass source explained.

cases.title: Distillation enriches a volatile component
cases.original_physical_forecast: Distilling 10% of an ethanol/water mixture should enrich ethanol in the receiver and conserve both components across vessels plus declared losses.

cases.title: Acid curdles milk without inventing protein molecules
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acidifying milk should show aggregation/curdling or a clear protein-model boundary, and retain unresolved milk mass.

cases.title: A peroxide catalyst has an explicit model boundary
cases.original_physical_forecast: MnO2 added to dilute hydrogen peroxide should yield oxygen and catalytic turnover or explicitly say kinetics/catalysis is unavailable; silence would fail.

cases.title: Waiting is not permission to teleport matter
cases.original_physical_forecast: Waiting one hour with dilute NaCl at room temperature should conserve dissolved salt and avoid spontaneous precipitation or chemical conversion; any evaporation must be accounted.

cases.title: Boyle syringe comparison
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal gas doses at equal temperature produce twice the absolute pressure in half the headspace.

cases.title: Venting releases compression
cases.original_physical_forecast: Opening removes imposed compression and exchanges gas with the environment.

cases.title: Hydrogen pop positive
cases.original_physical_forecast: Hydrogen headspace gives a positive pop test; test should not produce oxygen spontaneously.

cases.title: Oxygen glowing splint positive
cases.original_physical_forecast: Oxygen supports combustion and relights a glowing splint.

cases.title: Nitrogen glowing splint negative
cases.original_physical_forecast: Nitrogen cannot relight a glowing splint.

cases.title: Carbon dioxide limewater positive
cases.original_physical_forecast: Carbon dioxide clouds limewater via carbonate formation.

cases.title: Ammonia damp litmus basic
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ammonia gas dissolves on damp litmus and gives an alkaline response.

cases.title: Cooling inert solid without phase crossing
cases.original_physical_forecast: One kJ removed from one mole iron lowers its temperature tens of kelvin without changing material mass.

cases.title: Two-stage sensible heat cycle
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding then removing equal heat below any phase transition returns copper to its starting state.

cases.title: Energy split invariance for copper
cases.original_physical_forecast: Without a phase crossing or reactions, splitting the same total input energy leaves the same final state.

cases.title: Equivalent molar and gram dose
cases.original_physical_forecast: Mass and mole input units describe the same iron inventory within atomic-weight rounding.

cases.title: Daniell cell responds to copper-ion activity
cases.original_physical_forecast: Increasing Cu(II) activity tenfold at fixed Zn(II) activity increases the Daniell emf by about 29.6mV at 298K. Absolute ideal-standard voltage is around1.10V; sulfate complexation and activity corrections can shift it.

cases.title: Identical copper half-cells cancel their standard potential
cases.original_physical_forecast: Two identical Cu/Cu(II) half-cells at the same temperature have zero emf. Choosing a nonzero standard copper potential twice must cancel.

cases.title: A concentration cell works without two different metals
cases.original_physical_forecast: Cu/Cu(II) electrodes with a tenfold Cu(II) activity difference form a concentration cell: ideal emf magnitude29.6mV at298K, despite identical electrode metals.

cases.title: Reading a galvanic voltage is not an arbitrary discharge
cases.original_physical_forecast: A potential measurement alone has no specified load or discharge duration. Repeated readings should not prescribe arbitrary zinc consumption/copper deposition; a real current-transfer model would require an explicit circuit and electron ledger.

cases.title: Manganese dioxide accelerates peroxide decomposition without being spent as fuel
cases.original_physical_forecast: MnO2 can catalyze H2O2 decomposition:2H2O2→2H2O+O2. It should accelerate the finite-time oxygen release relative to the catalyst-free control without being consumed stoichiometrically.

cases.title: Filter a dissolved electrolyte away from an inert mineral suspension
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ordinary filtration retains particulate silica and passes water with dissolved sodium chloride. It must not treat all initially added solids as permanently filterable.

cases.title: A colorless metal salt should not acquire a fabricated visible spectrum
cases.original_physical_forecast: A dilute zinc sulfate solution is colorless in the visible range because Zn(II) has no visible d-d transition. This does not establish that its complete UV spectrum is zero.

cases.title: Evaporative concentration eventually leaves a conserved salt residue
cases.original_physical_forecast: Removing 90% of solvent can make the remaining brine supersaturated and leave NaCl crystals. Sodium and chloride remain in the vessel; lost mass is attributable to escaped water, not salt.

cases.title: Magnetic separation distinguishes iron filings from copper particles
cases.original_physical_forecast: A magnet attracts iron much more strongly than ordinary copper. The separation moves iron inventory while copper remains behind, without a chemical reaction.

cases.title: Distillation should reject a nonvolatile electrolyte from the condensate
cases.original_physical_forecast: An ideal still carries volatile water into the receiver while sodium chloride stays in the pot. Salt concentration in the residue rises; entrainment is a separate mechanism, not implied by distillation.

cases.title: Fresh small solvent portions outperform one extraction with the same total solvent
cases.original_physical_forecast: At the same distribution coefficient and total organic volume, several fresh equilibrium extractions remove more dissolved iodine than a single contact. Iodine conservation must hold separately for the two independent preparations.

cases.title: An acid-base indicator should reverse color after stoichiometric neutralization
cases.original_physical_forecast: Phenolphthalein is pink in a moderately alkaline solution and loses that color when an equal strong-acid dose removes the excess hydroxide. Indicator dye is not irreversibly destroyed by this ordinary pH cycle.

cases.title: Carbonate acidification distinguishes bicarbonate storage from escaped carbon dioxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Carbonate needs two strong-acid equivalents per mole for complete conversion to neutral carbon dioxide, but a one-equivalent dose may instead leave dissolved bicarbonate. A mineral disappearing is therefore not by itself proof that all carbon escaped as CO2. The second acid dose drives the carbon balance toward CO2 while conserving calcium.

cases.title: Half-neutralized acetic acid should reveal a buffer before equivalence
cases.original_physical_forecast: At half equivalence, an acetic-acid/acetate buffer has pH near pKa, about 4.76 at 25C. At complete neutralization, sodium acetate is mildly alkaline rather than exactly neutral; the conserved analytical acetate pool is 0.01mol.

cases.title: Filtration retains chalk but passes dissolved salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: Chalk is poorly soluble near neutral pH while dilute sodium chloride dissolves. Filtration should collect chalk in the source and brine in the receiver. Filtering the clear filtrate back should return liquid and salt without manufacturing a second chalk cake.

cases.title: Precipitate filtration versus homogeneous neutralization
cases.original_physical_forecast: Copper sulfate plus two hydroxide equivalents forms insoluble copper hydroxide and an aqueous sodium sulfate phase; matched acid/base neutralization instead yields dissolved sodium chloride. A filter discriminates physical phase rather than calling all reaction products solids.

cases.title: Evaporation and captured distillation differ in bench ownership
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal water removal should leave similar concentrated brines. Distillation transfers condensate into a bench vessel; open evaporation removes water to surroundings, so the two bench material budgets differ even when pot states match.

cases.title: Sub-boiling sealed-water heat/cool cycle
cases.original_physical_forecast: A small positive energy raises the temperature of sealed liquid water. Removing the same energy reverses this single-phase excursion, with unchanged water inventory and total mass.

cases.title: One heat pulse versus four equal pulses
cases.original_physical_forecast: At unchanged composition below boiling, equal total supplied heat should give the same final state irrespective of splitting the energy into pulses, when commands introduce no additional elapsed cooling time.

cases.title: Water amount and heating energy doubled together
cases.original_physical_forecast: For water-dominated heat storage, doubling water amount and supplied energy preserves the temperature rise. The second sample has twice the water inventory and sample mass. Fixed vessel heat capacity can break exact thermal scaling and must be visible as a separate energy sink.

cases.title: Equal hot/cold water mixing versus direct midpoint preparation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Mixing equal amounts of the same liquid at 20 C and 40 C gives approximately 30 C and the same composition and mass as a directly prepared 100 mL sample at 30 C. Thermal expansion and weak heat-capacity variation allow small departures from the exact midpoint.

cases.title: Added inert gas pressure increment halves with doubled headspace
cases.original_physical_forecast: For an ideal inert gas at low density, equal added gas amounts produce pressure increments inversely proportional to headspace volume. Normalize pressure by measured absolute temperature and subtract each vessel baseline to remove initially trapped air.

cases.title: Gas amount and headspace scale together
cases.original_physical_forecast: Doubling gas amount and headspace preserves number density and the temperature-normalized added pressure. The added nitrogen mass doubles even if the pressure is unchanged.

cases.title: Sealed inert-gas temperature-pressure reversibility
cases.original_physical_forecast: At fixed headspace and fixed gas amount, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature. An equal heat/cool cycle restores the original gas state if no external loss or phase change occurs.

cases.title: Repeated gas measurements must not consume or heat the sample
cases.original_physical_forecast: Pressure, temperature and balance observations of a sealed inert sample are non-destructive and should commute without changing the material or energy ledger.

cases.title: Acid/base order equivalence
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal acid and base inventories end near neutral in either order; order must not create different salt inventories. Thermal uncertainty must remain explicit.

cases.title: Tenfold strong-acid dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding nine initial solvent volumes raises dilute strong-acid pH by roughly1 without removing acid or chloride.

cases.title: Tenfold strong-base dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Tenfold dilution lowers dilute strong-base pH by roughly1 without neutralising or removing sodium.

cases.title: Pouring dilution versus direct water addition
cases.original_physical_forecast: The same acid and total water reached by a pour or direct addition give equivalent dilute pH and solvent/solute inventories.

cases.title: Silver chloride precipitation order
cases.original_physical_forecast: Both orders make predominantly solid silver chloride with equal final elemental inventories.

cases.title: Chloride limits silver chloride yield
cases.original_physical_forecast: One chloride equivalent limits AgCl to roughly0.001mol and leaves substantial dissolved excess silver.

cases.title: Common chloride ion suppresses silver chloride dissolution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Added chloride suppresses dissolved silver fromAgCl compared with purewater; remaining solid is not absent chemistry.

cases.title: Repeated filtration cannot duplicate precipitate
cases.original_physical_forecast: A second filtration of the first filtrate cannot reproduce the first solid dose. Dissolved material and solvent follow the filtrate while precipitate remains separated.

cases.title: Barium sulfate precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equimolar barium and sulfate produce almost quantitative white BaSO4 precipitate. Unsupported ingredient/phase must be distinguished from soluble product.

cases.title: Carbonate acid-dose ladder
cases.original_physical_forecast: Sequential acid cannot exceed its proton budget or erase carbon; later equivalents shift bicarbonate towardCO2 without duplicate doses.

cases.title: Acid dissolves calcite with retained carbon
cases.original_physical_forecast: Enough acid dissolves most calcite intoCa2+ and carbon dioxide/carbonic species in a sealed vessel.

cases.title: Too little acid cannot erase a calcite stock
cases.original_physical_forecast: A tenth of the two-equivalent acid requirement dissolves only part of the calcite; it cannot vanish wholesale.

cases.title: Copper hydroxide consumes two hydroxide equivalents
cases.original_physical_forecast: Copper(II) plustwohydroxides forms a blue hydroxide solid; leftover sulfate and sodium remain accounted.

cases.title: Ferric hydroxide consumes three hydroxide equivalents
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ferric iron precipitates a hydroxide/oxyhydroxide with three hydroxide equivalents without spontaneous Fe metal production.

cases.title: Magnet separates iron from silica
cases.original_physical_forecast: An ordinary magnetic separation moves magnetic solid iron but leaves silica in its original vessel and cannot create material.

cases.title: Magnet cannot convert ferric solution into iron metal
cases.original_physical_forecast: Dissolved ferric ions are not a ferromagnetic metal grain; magnetic separation must not reduce ions toFe or remove arbitrary solutionstock.

cases.title: Gas pressure versus volume
cases.original_physical_forecast: For equal final gas amount and temperature, pressure in 500 mL should be about twice that in 1 L. For a fresh seal that includes ambient air, compare nitrogen partial pressures or added-pressure increments; added N2 contributions are about 24.8 and 49.6 kPa.

cases.title: Heating sealed gas
cases.original_physical_forecast: If heat raises reported gas temperature and volume/inventory stay fixed, pressure should rise in the same ratio as absolute temperature: Pafter/Pbefore=(Tafter+273.15)/(Tbefore+273.15), within 10%. No exact temperature rise is assumed because vessel heat capacity is unspecified.

cases.title: Gas pressure versus amount
cases.original_physical_forecast: At stable temperature, each dose adds approximately 12.4 kPa to pressure; allow 10–15 kPa. The two increments should agree within 15%, accounting for reported temperature shifts.

cases.title: Opening a pressurized vessel
cases.original_physical_forecast: Initial pressure should exceed ambient substantially; after opening, overpressure should disappear and any reported pressure should be about ambient (90–110 kPa at a standard bench). Gas inventory may fall or be treated as exchanged with atmosphere.

cases.title: Magnetic iron sulfur separation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Receiver v2 should be enriched in Fe relative to the original 1:1 mass ratio. Most Fe should transfer and most sulfur remain; a receiver Fe:S mass ratio above 5 is a useful pass target when amounts are available.

cases.title: Oxygen splint test
cases.original_physical_forecast: An oxygen-enriched sample should give a positive glowing-splint/reignition response; the nitrogen-enriched control should not. Trapped ambient air may weaken a strict negative control; evaluate final composition from inspect.

cases.title: Hydrogen pop test specificity
cases.original_physical_forecast: Hydrogen should give a positive pop identification when the test introduces suitable air/oxygen; CO2 should give a negative pop. No sustained CO2 combustion is expected. If the test requires preexisting oxygen and sealed vessels contain none, hydrogen negativity is inconclusive.

cases.title: Water sensible heating
cases.original_physical_forecast: The final water temperature should rise by approximately 2.4 C; allow 1.5–3.5 C for ordinary vessel heat capacity. Water remains liquid, with essentially unchanged inventory.

cases.title: Water sensible cooling
cases.original_physical_forecast: Temperature falls about 2.4 C; allow a fall of 1.5–3.5 C. Water remains liquid.

cases.title: Mass dependence of heating
cases.original_physical_forecast: Both warm; the 50 g sample warms more. Ideal rises are 4.8 and 2.4 C. The ratio of temperature rises should be approximately 2, with 1.4–2.6 acceptable if equal vessel heat capacities contribute.

cases.title: Hot and cold water mixing
cases.original_physical_forecast: A mixed temperature near 40 C, broadly 35–45 C allowing a vessel initially near ambient, and approximately 100 g of water.

cases.title: Electrolyte conductivity
cases.original_physical_forecast: Approximately 0.1 M NaCl should conduct far better than the water control; ideally around 5–15 mS/cm at room temperature if absolute units are reported. The sign and substantial increase are the primary observations.

cases.title: Strong acid dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Initial pH approximately 2 and diluted pH approximately 3. The pH increase should be 0.8–1.2; final liquid volume should be approximately 1 L if dilute specifies a target volume.

cases.title: Strong base dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: At approximately 25 C, pH starts near 12 and ends near 11; the drop should be 0.8–1.2.

cases.title: Stoichiometric neutralization
cases.original_physical_forecast: Initial pH near 2; final pH approximately 6–8 at room temperature. No persistent free HCl/NaOH excess should remain; Na+ and Cl- may be reported as ions or NaCl.

cases.title: Acid excess after neutralization
cases.original_physical_forecast: Approximately 0.001 mol acid equivalents remain in about 0.1 L, giving pH 1.7–2.3. The final solution remains acidic.

cases.title: Weak versus strong acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: For approximately 0.01 M solutions, HCl pH is near 2 while acetic acid is near 3.4 (allow 3.1–3.7). Acetic acid should be at least 0.8 pH unit higher.

cases.title: Salt saturation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Liquid brine and undissolved solid NaCl should coexist. Roughly 34–38 g dissolves per 100 g water, leaving approximately 12–16 g solid.

cases.title: Silver chloride precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: A white AgCl precipitate should appear, amount close to 0.001 mol (0.143 g; allow 0.12–0.15 g if quantified). Residual dissolved silver should be a small fraction of the input.

cases.title: Barium sulfate precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: White BaSO4 solid close to 0.001 mol (0.233 g; allow 0.21–0.24 g) should form.

cases.title: Calcium carbonate precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: White calcium carbonate precipitate should form, approaching 0.001 mol (0.100 g) if equilibrium is modeled. A broadly 0.07–0.11 g solid amount is acceptable.

cases.title: Copper hydroxide precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Blue Cu(OH)2 precipitate should form, close to 0.001 mol (0.098 g). Dissolved Cu(II) should decline substantially.

cases.title: Carbonate acid gas
cases.original_physical_forecast: CO2 generation and a positive limewater test are expected when the assay samples generated gas. Total generated CO2 across gas and dissolved pools is at most 0.001 mol. Remaining strong acid is about 0.001 mol, so pH should be roughly 2.

cases.title: Copper resists nonoxidizing acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: Copper should remain overwhelmingly metallic and no substantial H2 should be generated. No positive hydrogen pop attributable to this mixture is expected.

cases.title: Iron displaces copper
cases.original_physical_forecast: Copper metal should appear, the dissolved blue Cu(II) pool should decline, and some Fe(II) should appear. Cu production cannot exceed 0.001 mol; complete reaction consumes 0.001 mol Fe.

cases.title: Copper displaces silver
cases.original_physical_forecast: Silver metal should appear and dissolved Cu(II) should increase. Complete conversion gives 0.002 mol Ag (0.216 g) while consuming 0.001 mol Cu.

cases.title: Carbon dioxide acidifies water
cases.original_physical_forecast: Water pH should decline and become acidic, ordinarily around 3.5–5.5 at this CO2 loading. Some CO2 should be dissolved if gas-liquid equilibrium is supported.

cases.title: Ammonia basifies water
cases.original_physical_forecast: Water should become alkaline. If most ammonia dissolves, about 0.01 M total ammonia gives pH near 10.6; broadly pH 9–11.5 is reasonable given partitioning.

cases.title: Filtration of sand suspension
cases.original_physical_forecast: Receiver v2 should contain liquid water and little insoluble SiO2; at least 90% of the initial silica should be excluded from filtrate if the filter represents an ordinary solid/liquid separator. Silica may remain in v1 or be separately recorded as filter residue.

cases.title: Decanting supernatant
cases.original_physical_forecast: Approximately half the available supernatant liquid should transfer, broadly 40–60 mL, with most settled silica remaining in v1 if settling and decanting are represented. Receiver should be depleted in solid relative to source.

cases.title: Partial evaporation concentrates salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: Water should decline roughly by half if the fraction denotes liquid evaporation; NaCl should remain near 1 g. Concentration should rise to approximately twice its initial value while remaining far below saturation. Evaluate concentration from reported inventories if fraction semantics differ.

cases.title: Distilling salt water
cases.original_physical_forecast: Receiver should gain water and be strongly depleted in NaCl, normally with less than 1% of the initial salt. Receiver conductivity should be low compared with brine; roughly 10–30 mL collected is expected if fraction is initial liquid fraction.

cases.title: Charge bounded aqueous electrolysis
cases.original_physical_forecast: If inert-electrode water electrolysis is supported, H2 and O2 should be produced in approximately 2:1 molar ratio. With Q=1 C, maxima are 5.18e-6 mol H2 and 2.59e-6 mol O2 at 100% current efficiency; dissolved gas and headspace gas must be summed. Water consumption is tiny.

cases.title: Bounded acid base titration
cases.original_physical_forecast: If 1 mL means aliquot size and max means number of aliquots, the endpoint should occur at about 10 mL of 0.1 M NaOH, within one 1 mL increment. If until ph 7 uses a crossing condition, final pH should be at least 7 and may overshoot; inventories should show about 0.001–0.0011 mol added hydroxide.

cases.title: Bicarbonate vinegar effervescence
cases.original_physical_forecast: CO2 should form, up to 0.001 mol across phases, and residual mixture should contain acetate plus unconsumed acetic acid. After CO2 loss the equal acetate/acid buffer would have pH near 4.76; dissolved CO2 can lower it. Broad final pH 4–6 is expected.

cases.title: Limewater test for carbon dioxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: White cloudiness from calcium carbonate.

cases.title: Protolysis of hydrogen chloride in water
cases.original_physical_forecast: An acidic, ion-containing solution forms.

cases.title: Ammonia as a base in water
cases.original_physical_forecast: The solution is alkaline.

cases.title: Chloride test by silver chloride precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: A white precipitate forms.

cases.title: Sulfate test by barium sulfate precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: A white precipitate forms.

cases.title: Acetic-acid protolysis / acetate buffer
cases.original_physical_forecast: Only part of the acid is deprotonated.

cases.title: Autoprotolysis of water
cases.original_physical_forecast: A small equilibrium population of hydronium and hydroxide exists.

cases.title: Hydrogencarbonate with acid: effervescence and leavening
cases.original_physical_forecast: Carbon dioxide bubbles form.

cases.title: Ammonium test with hydroxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ammonia is released and can be detected without direct smelling.

cases.title: First protolysis of sulfuric acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: Hydrogensulfate and hydronium form.

cases.title: Calcium carbonate precipitation from ions
cases.original_physical_forecast: Calcium carbonate precipitates.

cases.title: Limestone–carbon dioxide equilibrium
cases.original_physical_forecast: Limestone can dissolve; CO2 loss favours reverse precipitation.

cases.title: Acid decomposition of thiosulfate
cases.original_physical_forecast: Sulfur particles cause cloudiness; sulfur dioxide can be released.

cases.title: F01-water
cases.original_physical_forecast: Neutral solvent baseline; no added acid/base or reaction product.

cases.title: F02-HCl
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acidic pH compared with water baseline.

cases.title: F03-NaOH
cases.original_physical_forecast: Alkaline pH compared with water baseline.

cases.title: F04-neutralisation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal strong acid/base returns toward neutral pH; inspect heating separately, no empirical heat calibration.

cases.title: F05-NH4Cl
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ammonium-salt solution acidic, rather than ammonia-like alkalinity.

cases.title: F06-Na2CO3
cases.original_physical_forecast: Carbonate-salt solution alkaline; carbonate/hydrocarbonate solution species available.

cases.title: F08-CaCO3-HCl
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid-driven carbonate dissolution and CO2 generation; distinguish vented gas from retained inventory.

cases.title: F09-CuO-HCl
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid promotes CuO dissolution and dissolved copper; compare with pre-acid inspection.

cases.title: F10-CO2-NaOH
cases.original_physical_forecast: Base captures CO2 into carbonate/bicarbonate; inspect pH and distinguish initial-air carbon.

cases.title: Conductometric strong-acid titration: a minimum, not only an endpoint
cases.original_physical_forecast: Conductivity falls as highly mobile hydrogen ions are replaced by sodium ions, reaches a minimum near equivalence, and rises with excess hydroxide.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The equivalence snapshot has lower conductivity than both the initial acid and final excess-base snapshots.
pH crosses from acidic to near-neutral to alkaline; conductivity does not become zero.

cases.title: Weak-acid conductometric titration distinguishes neutralisation from dilution
cases.original_physical_forecast: Formation of sodium acetate increases the mobile-ion inventory; after equivalence, excess hydroxide gives a steeper conductivity rise.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Conductivity at equivalence exceeds its initial weak-acid value.
The final equal-size base addition gives a stronger conductivity response than an equal-size addition well before equivalence; inspect actual volumes.

cases.title: Resolve the first two phosphoric-acid equivalence regions
cases.original_physical_forecast: The pH curve contains separate first- and second-proton neutralisation regions; half-equivalent mixtures reveal two different buffers.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: pH increases across the four additions, with materially separated buffer regions.
Track total phosphorus through H3PO4, H2PO4-, HPO4(2-) and any further species; it remains 0.001 mol.

cases.title: Sulfuric acid needs two base equivalents per formula unit
cases.original_physical_forecast: One equivalent leaves bisulfate acidity; two equivalents give a sulfate-dominated solution without a large strong-acid reserve.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The one-equivalent mixture is acidic, and the second equivalent produces a substantial pH rise.
Sulfur inventory is conserved; the final solution need not have exactly pH 7.000.

cases.title: Bicarbonate is amphiprotic, unlike strongly basic carbonate
cases.original_physical_forecast: At equal analytical carbon loading, bicarbonate is moderately basic and carbonate is appreciably more alkaline.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: pH(v2) exceeds pH(v1).
Account for any CO2 exchange; do not confuse equal carbon loading with equal sodium concentration.

cases.title: Build an ammonium–ammonia buffer by half-neutralisation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Half-neutralisation creates an NH4+/NH3 buffer. A small acid challenge changes its ratio rather than causing an unbuffered pH collapse.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Both ammonium and ammonia remain after half-neutralisation.
The acid pulse reduces pH while leaving a mixed buffer; include headspace ammonia in the nitrogen balance.

cases.title: An acetate buffer absorbs hydroxide by spending its acid component
cases.original_physical_forecast: Hydroxide consumes acetic acid and raises the acetate/acid ratio, causing only a moderate pH increase.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Acetic-acid inventory falls and acetate inventory rises without loss of total organic-acid carbon.
The pH remains in an acidic buffer region rather than becoming strongly alkaline.

cases.title: Equal buffer pH does not mean equal buffer capacity
cases.original_physical_forecast: The buffers start at similar pH, but the ten-times larger acid/base pool resists the same acid challenge more effectively.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Initial pH values are close, without demanding identity at different ionic strengths.
The concentrated buffer has the smaller absolute pH shift.

cases.title: Similar initial pH can conceal very different acid reserves
cases.original_physical_forecast: These doses give roughly similar initial pH in an ideal calculation. The base challenge exhausts the strong-acid dose while leaving acetic acid in a buffer.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: After the challenge, the HCl vessel is alkaline and the acetic-acid vessel remains acidic.
Do not treat the approximate initial pH match as an exact calibration.

cases.title: A conjugate-base salt hydrolyses even with no added alkali
cases.original_physical_forecast: Sodium acetate solution is more alkaline than a sodium chloride control because acetate accepts protons from water.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: pH(v1) exceeds the near-neutral control.
The model shows some acetic acid and hydroxide rather than creation of sodium hydroxide as a separate bottle species.

cases.title: A phosphate buffer protects near-neutral pH
cases.original_physical_forecast: A phosphate mixture between its first and second neutralisation equivalents resists an acid pulse that strongly acidifies water.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The phosphate vessel retains both H2PO4- and HPO4(2-) after the acid pulse.
Its absolute pH shift is smaller than the water control’s.

cases.title: Mixing pH values is not taking their arithmetic mean
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal volumes of approximately pH 2 and pH 4 strong acid mix to about pH 2.3 in the ideal approximation, not pH 3.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The mixed pH is substantially closer to the more acidic starting solution.
The total strong-acid amount is the sum of both additions; allow activity corrections in the numerical estimate.

cases.title: Hydroxide equivalents depend on formula stoichiometry
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal formula-unit amounts of NaOH and Ca(OH)2 consume different proton amounts: one and two equivalents respectively.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The NaOH vessel retains strong-acid excess, while the calcium-hydroxide vessel is much closer to neutral.
The calcium dose should dissolve in the supplied acid; no extra uncounted base is assumed.

cases.title: Compare antacid capacity per gram without confusing fizz with neutralisation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Both solids consume two protons per formula unit, but the smaller molar mass of Mg(OH)2 gives greater acid capacity per gram. Only carbonate produces CO2.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The magnesium-hydroxide vessel has less residual acidity than the equal-mass carbonate vessel.
CO2 generation is associated with carbonate, not required for every antacid reaction.

cases.title: Zinc hydroxide precipitates, then dissolves in excess base
cases.original_physical_forecast: A moderate hydroxide dose gives Zn(OH)2; sufficiently strong excess hydroxide can redissolve it into soluble hydroxo-zinc species.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: A zinc-bearing hydroxide solid appears at the intermediate snapshot.
Its amount decreases after excess base while total zinc remains constant; unsupported hydroxo-complex coverage is not a chemical pass.

cases.title: Dissolve magnesium hydroxide and reprecipitate it
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid dissolves the initial hydroxide; restoring alkalinity produces a magnesium hydroxide solid again without inventing a magnesium-chloride bottle key.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The solid inventory falls on acidification and rises again after base addition.
Total magnesium stays at 0.001 mol across the cycle.

cases.title: Ferric hydroxide redissolves when its pH support is removed
cases.original_physical_forecast: Brown ferric hydroxide formed by base addition is substantially removed by a deliberate excess of acid.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Ferric solid decreases after the acid challenge.
Iron remains in the vessel in dissolved forms; disappearance of turbidity is not disappearance of iron.

cases.title: An acid reserve can prevent calcium carbonate precipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Without prior acid, carbonate precipitates calcium. With excess proton capacity, carbonate is protonated and the calcium mostly remains dissolved.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The unacidified vessel has more calcium-carbonate solid.
Account for acid consumption and carbon leaving the open acidified vessel as CO2.

cases.title: Limewater clouds and then clears under excess carbon dioxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Initial CO2 converts hydroxide into calcium carbonate; excess retained CO2 lowers pH and favours dissolved calcium/bicarbonate.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: A calcium-carbonate maximum occurs at the intermediate stage.
The final solid fraction is lower, with carbon and calcium accounted for across all phases.

cases.title: Purify impure limestone by dissolution and reprecipitation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid dissolves the calcium carbonate, filtration rejects sand, and carbonate addition recovers a calcium-rich precipitate in the receiver.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Most SiO2 remains in v1 during filtration.
A calcium-carbonate solid reappears in v2; compare recovered calcium, not total crude solid mass.

cases.title: Convert copper oxide through a soluble salt to a hydroxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid dissolves black copper oxide; subsequent base addition forms a copper hydroxide-rich solid while preserving copper inventory.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The initial oxide decreases after acid addition.
The final precipitate is identified by composition, not assumed to be unchanged CuO simply because copper stayed in the vessel.

cases.title: Zinc reduces two silver ions per atom oxidised
cases.original_physical_forecast: Zinc oxidation supplies two electrons per zinc atom, so the stoichiometric ceiling is two silver atoms deposited per zinc atom consumed.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Identify metallic silver rather than a silver salt precipitate.
Compare zinc oxidation and silver deposition in electron equivalents; the nominal ceiling is 0.002 mol Ag.

cases.title: An active metal releases hydrogen from acid; copper is the control
cases.original_physical_forecast: Magnesium can reduce protons to hydrogen. Copper does not evolve hydrogen through the same proton-displacement reaction under ordinary non-oxidising conditions.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Require chemically identified H2, not a pressure rise alone, in the magnesium vessel.
The copper control should not show corresponding proton-reduction H2; possible oxygen-driven copper corrosion is a different pathway.

cases.title: Iodometric stoichiometry uses two thiosulfates per iodine
cases.original_physical_forecast: Thiosulfate reduces iodine to iodide; half the required dose should leave an oxidised-iodine pool, while the full nominal dose removes most of it.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Track oxidised iodine across I2 and any I3- representation.
Compare thiosulfate consumption with iodine reduction using a 2:1 molar relationship and look for tetrathionate, not sulfate assumed by name.

cases.title: Ascorbic acid reduces iodine with a one-to-one molecular budget
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ascorbic acid is oxidised to dehydroascorbic acid as the oxidised iodine pool is reduced.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: An iodine decrease is accompanied by formation of the modelled oxidised vitamin-C product.
The nominal molecular redox ratio is one ascorbic acid per iodine; account for any iodine complexes.

cases.title: Vitamin C has finite reducing capacity: iodine eventually persists
cases.original_physical_forecast: Successive iodine additions consume a finite ascorbic-acid pool. Iodine persists after that pool is exhausted.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Early iodine additions are reduced while ascorbic acid remains.
The final addition leaves an oxidised-iodine excess without regenerating consumed ascorbic acid.

cases.title: Acidified permanganate oxidises oxalic acid to carbon dioxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Under a chemically appropriate acidic, warm setup, permanganate is reduced while oxalic-acid carbon becomes CO2.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Look for oxidised carbon and manganese(II) rather than assuming simple purple dilution.
The nominal stoichiometric ratio is 5 oxalic acids to 2 permanganates.

cases.title: Changing the zinc half-cell shifts Daniell voltage in the opposite direction
cases.original_physical_forecast: Increasing zinc-ion activity with the copper side otherwise fixed lowers the forward Zn/Cu cell voltage according to the reaction quotient.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The second open-circuit voltage is lower in the same electrode order.
No bulk discharge or metal consumption is inferred from a voltage measurement alone.

cases.title: A copper–silver cell links two different electron stoichiometries
cases.original_physical_forecast: The silver electrode is the more positive reduction half-cell; copper oxidation coupled to silver reduction has a positive forward driving force.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Identify which electrode is positive using the runtime sign convention rather than guessing the order of printed signs.
Only open-circuit potential is expected; no two-silver-per-copper discharge is performed by cell.

cases.title: Electrolysis connects charge to the hydrogen–oxygen gas ratio
cases.original_physical_forecast: For water electrolysis with a spectator sulfate electrolyte, net generated hydrogen and oxygen should have a 2:1 molar ratio and obey Faraday’s law.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Subtract the sealed-air baseline and sum dissolved plus headspace product increments.
For Q = 10 C, ideal ceilings are Q/(2F) mol H2 and Q/(4F) mol O2; unsupported electrode routing is not a pass.

cases.title: Dalton additivity after subtracting the sealed-air baseline
cases.original_physical_forecast: At approximately constant headspace and temperature, the pressure increments from added gases are approximately additive, with small gas-solubility differences.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare pressure increments rather than treating the initial headspace as a vacuum.
Use the actual gas-phase moles and temperature in P = nRT/V; O2 and N2 need not dissolve equally.

cases.title: Dissolution makes carbon dioxide and nitrogen pressurise differently
cases.original_physical_forecast: More added CO2 is accommodated by dissolved inorganic-carbon species than an equal N2 dose, changing the pressure increment.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare gas-phase fractions of the added material, not pressure alone.
The CO2 vessel should store more of the dose in the liquid under these conditions.

cases.title: Chemical absorption lowers carbon-dioxide headspace pressure
cases.original_physical_forecast: The alkaline liquid converts CO2 into bicarbonate/carbonate, storing more carbon in liquid and reducing the CO2 contribution to pressure.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare carbon partition fractions at the actual temperatures.
The alkaline vessel retains the added carbon; pressure reduction alone must not be mistaken for carbon deletion.

cases.title: An acid trap captures ammonia as ammonium
cases.original_physical_forecast: Protonation stores ammonia as ammonium and reduces the uncharged ammonia fraction available to the headspace.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The acid trap has a larger ammonium fraction and a smaller gas-phase NH3 fraction.
All added nitrogen is accounted for in each vessel; the acidified solution need not become neutral.

cases.title: Capture carbon dioxide and release the same carbon again
cases.original_physical_forecast: Base captures the CO2 dose as inorganic-carbon ions; acidification reverses that storage and moves carbon back toward molecular and gas-phase CO2.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Carbonate/bicarbonate decline after acidification while headspace CO2 increases.
Total carbon is conserved across the capture–release cycle, apart from explicitly recorded initial air contributions.

cases.title: Degassing hard water promotes calcium-carbonate scale
cases.original_physical_forecast: Removing CO2 from a bicarbonate-rich calcium solution favours renewed calcium-carbonate precipitation.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: First verify that the CO2-rich stage dissolved a measurable calcium fraction.
After sweeping, check for increased calcium-carbonate solid and include swept carbon in the balance.

cases.title: Catalyst particle size changes surface-controlled peroxide decomposition
cases.original_physical_forecast: At equal catalyst amount, smaller modelled particles expose more surface and consume more peroxide during the same virtual interval.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The finer-particle vessel has less residual peroxide at equal elapsed time.
MnO2 amount remains unchanged; particle size, not catalyst quantity, is the independent variable.

cases.title: Moderate warming accelerates the same manganese-dioxide reaction
cases.original_physical_forecast: The warmer heterogeneous-catalyst mixture reacts faster over a common short interval.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The warm vessel retains less peroxide at the shared timepoint.
Use measured temperatures after additions; added reagents and reaction heat can shift nominal starting temperatures.

cases.title: The enzyme temperature response has an activity envelope
cases.original_physical_forecast: The source model predicts acceleration from room temperature to moderate warmth, but suppression in very hot water due to its enzyme-activity envelope.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Early peroxide conversion is greater at moderate warmth than at room temperature.
The very-hot case is slower than the moderately warm case; this is not a test of irreversible denaturation history.

cases.title: Recover and reuse manganese dioxide with a fresh substrate charge
cases.original_physical_forecast: The retained solid catalyst remains active when supplied with fresh solvent and peroxide.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The catalyst amount in v1 is not spent by the first reaction or created by reuse.
The second peroxide charge undergoes decomposition; do not equate rates unless temperature and retained-liquid conditions match.

cases.title: Acid activity, not acid bottle amount, controls a sulfur clock
cases.original_physical_forecast: Equal formal amounts of strong and weak acid give different proton activities and therefore different early thiosulfate-decomposition rates.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare starting pH and sulfur production in both vessels at a common time.
The more strongly acidic mixture should generally produce sulfur faster; match total thiosulfate loading.

cases.title: Warming accelerates acid decomposition of thiosulfate
cases.original_physical_forecast: With similar acidity and substrate loading, the warmer mixture produces sulfur more rapidly over an early common interval.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare residual thiosulfate and generated sulfur, not turbidity labels alone.
Check measured temperatures and pH to avoid attributing every difference to temperature alone.

cases.title: A second substrate pulse restarts an enzyme without adding new enzyme
cases.original_physical_forecast: The finite first substrate dose is consumed, but the enzyme remains available to process a second dose.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The second dose is consumed without a second catalase addition.
Catalase inventory remains fixed while cumulative substrate turnover exceeds the enzyme amount by many orders of magnitude.

cases.title: Equimolar esterification reaches equilibrium instead of complete conversion
cases.original_physical_forecast: The declared ideal-mixture K ≈ 4 model predicts partial esterification, approximately two-thirds conversion for initially product-free equimolar reactants.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Both ester and unreacted acid/alcohol remain after the command.
Evaluate Q from the actual represented reactant and product amounts; the two-thirds value is an ideal-model guide, not an observed yield.

cases.title: Alcohol excess shifts esterification at fixed acid loading
cases.original_physical_forecast: The alcohol-rich mixture should convert a larger fraction of its fixed acetic-acid dose into ester under the ideal equilibrium model.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare ester amount per initial acid amount, not ester concentration in unequal volumes.
Both simulations conserve the separately supplied total carbon and oxygen.

cases.title: Added product water suppresses esterification
cases.original_physical_forecast: Including water on the product side lowers equilibrium ester formation relative to the initially dry control.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The water-added vessel forms less ester per initial acid amount.
The comparison uses total initial plus generated water, not only newly produced water.

cases.title: Base-limited ester hydrolysis leaves residual ester
cases.original_physical_forecast: The nominal hydroxide dose can hydrolyse at most half the ester through the saponification reaction, producing acetate and ethanol.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Ester remains after the available hydroxide-equivalent budget has been spent.
Any conversion must match formation of both acetate and ethanol; a pH change alone is insufficient.

cases.title: Ester-limited hydrolysis leaves excess base
cases.original_physical_forecast: A sufficiently large hydroxide budget can exhaust the ester while leaving an alkaline product solution.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The ester inventory approaches its modelled completion limit with appropriate acetate and ethanol formation.
The remaining base budget differs from the base-limited case; inspect acid/base speciation rather than looking for a NaOH molecule count alone.

cases.title: Explicit alcohol oxidation is a requested model, not spontaneous vinegar formation
cases.original_physical_forecast: The explicit request converts ethanol and available oxygen into an acetic-acid/water product pool; the otherwise matched vessel has no organism or oxidation command.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The requested vessel shows the named stoichiometric conversion relative to its pre-command state.
The no-command control is not assumed to ferment; no measured reaction heat, rate or acetaldehyde mechanism is inferred.

cases.title: Overall glucose respiration preserves the six-carbon budget
cases.original_physical_forecast: The requested overall transformation can convert one glucose into six CO2 and six water molecules when oxygen is sufficient.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare glucose consumption with total new inorganic carbon across liquid and gas; the ratio is six carbons per glucose.
Oxygen consumption follows six per glucose, with no ATP, cellular mechanism or metabolic heat inferred.

cases.title: Successive distillate cuts become poorer in ethanol
cases.original_physical_forecast: The earlier vapour cut is normally richer in the more volatile ethanol than a later cut from the depleted pot.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare ethanol mole fractions in v2 and v3, not their unequal absolute amounts.
Each fractional cut applies to the then-remaining feed; reconcile all three vessel inventories.

cases.title: Redistillation enriches a volatile component but sacrifices recovery
cases.original_physical_forecast: Redistilling the first condensate increases ethanol fraction in the second condensate, while only part of the original ethanol reaches the final receiver.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Final-receiver ethanol fraction exceeds that of its feed.
Calculate final ethanol recovery against the initial 10 g dose, and include both residual pots in the balance.

cases.title: A filter cannot separate two miscible liquids
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ideal filtration transfers the homogeneous ethanol–water liquid without selectively retaining one molecular liquid as a solid.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The receiver composition matches the transferred liquid feed within numerical tolerance.
No ethanol-rich filter cake is invented; non-volatility and filtration are different selection rules.

cases.title: Separate iron, sand and salt with three different physical operations
cases.original_physical_forecast: Magnetic collection isolates iron, filtration leaves a sand-rich residue, and evaporation recovers salt from the dissolved fraction.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Assign the main iron, silica and sodium/chloride inventories to their intended final vessels.
Include the remaining mother liquor and removed water; recovered crystals do not need to equal the full initial salt dose.

cases.title: Determine chloride gravimetrically from a calcium-chloride sample
cases.original_physical_forecast: Two chlorides per calcium-chloride formula unit can yield nearly 0.002 mol AgCl, while a small silver excess remains in the filtrate.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Use identified dry AgCl amount to infer chloride, not the original formula-unit amount of CaCl2.
The ideal AgCl mass is approximately 0.2866 g before solubility or retained-liquid corrections; calcium remains mainly dissolved.

cases.title: Both sugar and salt pass a filter, but only one is a strong electrolyte
cases.original_physical_forecast: Both dissolved solutes transfer with water; salt gives much greater conductivity because dissolution is not the same as ionisation.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Both filtrates retain the corresponding dissolved solute inventory.
The salt filtrate conducts more strongly than the glucose filtrate without falsely calling glucose insoluble.

cases.title: A separating funnel drains the lower liquid layer, not every liquid
cases.original_physical_forecast: A resolved water/hexane two-phase mixture can be separated by draining its denser aqueous layer while the organic-rich layer remains.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Verify that the phase solver actually reported two liquid layers before judging the drain.
The receiver is water/salt-rich; iodine distribution is interpreted from phase composition rather than colour alone.

cases.title: Distillation simultaneously enriches ethanol and rejects salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: The distillate is ethanol-enriched relative to the starting liquid and strongly depleted in nonvolatile salt.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Assess ethanol enrichment and sodium/chloride rejection separately.
Close the ethanol, water and salt balances across both vessels; a pure-solvent condensate is not assumed.

cases.title: Equal masses of water and ethanol have different heat capacities
cases.original_physical_forecast: Below phase transitions, the same energy pulse raises the temperature of ethanol more than that of the same mass of water.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The ethanol temperature rise exceeds the water rise.
Neither case should cross its boiling point; compare energy per heat capacity, not just energy per mass.

cases.title: Hot copper and cold water equilibrate by heat capacity, not mass alone
cases.original_physical_forecast: The mixture should settle only a few degrees above the water’s initial temperature because water contributes much more heat capacity than the copper.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The final temperature is much closer to 20 C than to the mass-weighted value 46.7 C.
An ideal constant-heat-capacity estimate is about 23.5 C; compare with the model’s actual property values.

cases.title: Partial thawing spends heat without raising temperature
cases.original_physical_forecast: After creating an ice/water mixture, a smaller heating pulse melts part of the ice while the temperature stays near the melting point.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Ice decreases but is not exhausted by the partial reheating.
The mixture remains close to its melting plateau; pH of a fully homogeneous liquid is not presumed during phase coexistence.

cases.title: Ice formation concentrates the remaining brine
cases.original_physical_forecast: Freezing removes mostly water from the liquid phase, increasing the concentration of salt in the remaining brine without creating salt.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Some ice appears while a liquid brine remains.
Compare dissolved salt per liquid-water amount before and after; inspect any separate salt solid rather than assuming all salt must remain dissolved.

cases.title: Cooling a hot potassium-nitrate solution recovers crystals
cases.original_physical_forecast: The decrease in potassium-nitrate solubility on cooling can produce crystals from a hot, initially more highly dissolved feed.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Record dissolved and solid KNO3 before cooling; initial complete dissolution is checked rather than assumed.
Cooling increases the recovered crystal fraction without exceeding the initial potassium/nitrate inventory.

cases.title: Slaking lime couples chemical hydration to heat release
cases.original_physical_forecast: Calcium oxide reacts with water toward calcium hydroxide and an alkaline liquid; the real hydration reaction is exothermic.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Verify conversion of oxide into hydroxide/dissolved calcium species, not merely warming by an input-temperature difference.
A thermal claim requires an implemented heat contribution; missing reaction enthalpy is not evidence of an endothermic reaction.

cases.title: Heating bicarbonate generates carbonate, water and carbon dioxide
cases.original_physical_forecast: Crossing the curated thermal threshold converts bicarbonate toward carbonate with water and CO2 production; escaping products reduce the vessel’s retained mass.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Identify a carbonate product and account for carbon among retained solid and released CO2.
Mass loss depends on whether generated water also leaves; do not equate it automatically with CO2 alone.

cases.title: Ethanol’s boiling plateau is different from water’s
cases.original_physical_forecast: The energy pulse first reaches ethanol’s boiling region, then mainly drives vaporisation rather than heating all liquid far above its boiling point.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Temperature approaches the declared ethanol boiling plateau while retained liquid mass falls.
No combustion is inferred: heat and ignite are different operations.

cases.title: Salt dissolution can warm one solution and cool another
cases.original_physical_forecast: Under the documented dissolution-enthalpy model, calcium chloride warms the water while potassium chloride cools it.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Use each water temperature before salt addition as its own baseline.
Both solids substantially dissolve; opposite heat effects do not mean only one underwent a physical/chemical change.

cases.title: Neutralisation calorimetry must subtract prior dissolution heat
cases.original_physical_forecast: Mixing separately prepared acid and base solutions releases neutralisation heat in addition to the sensible heat already stored in those solutions.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare the mixed temperature with a heat-capacity-weighted no-reaction mixing baseline computed from the two pre-mix states.
Do not charge the earlier acid/base dissolution heat again as neutralisation heat; verify proton/hydroxide consumption.

cases.title: A common ammonium ion suppresses ammonia ionisation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding ammonium chloride lowers the pH of an otherwise equal ammonia dose by shifting its base equilibrium.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The NH3/NH4Cl mixture has lower pH than the ammonia-only mixture.
Both vessels retain their separately added total nitrogen when aqueous and headspace pools are summed.

cases.title: A basic buffer absorbs an alkali challenge
cases.original_physical_forecast: The buffered vessel shows a much smaller pH change than water receiving the same hydroxide dose.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare changes from each vessel’s own baseline, not just final pH.
The buffer retains ammonium after the challenge.

cases.title: Reverse a buffer ratio while holding its total pool constant
cases.original_physical_forecast: Reversing an approximately 1:9 base/acid ratio to 9:1 raises pH by roughly 1.9 units in the ideal approximation.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The acetate-rich mixture has higher pH.
Compare the measured difference with log10(81), allowing activity and temperature effects rather than imposing an exact equality.

cases.title: Diluting a buffer preserves its ratio but weakens capacity per volume
cases.original_physical_forecast: After splitting equal buffer inventories, dilution alone changes pH little. An equal acid challenge per approximate final litre consumes more of the buffer in the larger, dilute vessel.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The two pH values remain similar immediately after dilution.
Under the stated concentration-normalised acid challenge, the dilute vessel undergoes the larger pH decrease.

cases.title: An extremely dilute strong acid never becomes a base
cases.original_physical_forecast: Water autoionisation prevents the naive pH = -log10(c_acid) calculation from predicting pH 8 for a 10^-8 M acid addition.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The acid addition does not make the water more alkaline than its baseline.
Any neutral-pH estimate uses the actual temperature and boundary condition; atmospheric carbon may dominate a real sample.

cases.title: Weak-acid dilution increases the fraction ionised
cases.original_physical_forecast: On tenfold dilution the pH rises less than a full unit in the ordinary weak-acid regime while the ionised fraction of the acid increases.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare acetate divided by total acetate-family inventory before and after dilution.
Total acetic-acid-family amount remains constant even though concentration falls.

cases.title: Combine a weak-acid cation and weak-base anion
cases.original_physical_forecast: Comparable ammonium acidity and acetate basicity tend to give a near-neutral mixture while both weak equilibria remain active.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The final pH lies between corresponding ammonium-chloride-only and sodium-acetate-only expectations, rather than being strongly acidic or basic.
Account for ammonia partitioning and activity effects; near-neutral is not exactly pH 7.

cases.title: Metal-ion hydrolysis acidifies ferric chloride
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ferric-ion hydrolysis acidifies the water much more than calcium chloride does; hydroxide-bearing ferric species or solids may also appear.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The ferric vessel has lower pH than the calcium vessel.
Do not interpret any ferric hydroxide as evidence that hydroxide was added externally.

cases.title: A carbonate–bicarbonate buffer absorbs an acid pulse
cases.original_physical_forecast: A small proton dose mainly converts carbonate to bicarbonate, leaving an alkaline buffer rather than releasing all carbon as gas.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Bicarbonate increases relative to carbonate.
Total inorganic carbon across all phases remains 0.002 mol plus any declared initial boundary carbon.

cases.title: Neutral water need not have pH seven when warm
cases.original_physical_forecast: For a temperature-dependent water equilibrium, warmer pure water has a lower neutral pH while hydrogen and hydroxide activities remain matched.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Check neutrality from the hydrogen/hydroxide balance or pKw, not solely from proximity to seven.
If the model keeps a fixed dissociation constant, record that coverage limitation instead of claiming the expected thermal effect occurred.

cases.title: Excess ammonia can dissolve a copper hydroxide precipitate
cases.original_physical_forecast: Chemical expectation: excess ammonia stabilises dissolved copper ammine species and can remove the hydroxide precipitate, with a changed copper colour.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Require a decrease of copper-bearing solid together with a copper-ammine increase; colour alone does not establish complex formation.
Check copper and total nitrogen ownership, including headspace ammonia.

cases.title: Selective hydroxide precipitation separates ferric and cupric ions
cases.original_physical_forecast: A moderately acidic endpoint should preferentially remove ferric hydroxide while leaving much more copper in the filtrate.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: At the recorded endpoint, compare fractions of each metal in solid and dissolved pools.
The iron fraction retained in the source should exceed the copper fraction retained there; inspect endpoint overshoot and phases.

cases.title: Carbonate and sulfate precipitates respond differently to acid
cases.original_physical_forecast: Barium carbonate is acid-labile and can release CO2; barium sulfate should largely persist under the same dilute-acid challenge.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: First verify formation of each intended solid, including any witherite phase representation.
After acid addition, compare each solid with its own initial amount; carbonate loss should greatly exceed sulfate loss.

cases.title: Not every alkaline-earth sulfate precipitates at the same concentration
cases.original_physical_forecast: At these dilute analytical loadings, calcium sulfate is expected to remain mostly dissolved whereas barium sulfate precipitates strongly.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The barium vessel has a much larger fraction of its alkaline-earth metal in a sulfate solid.
A clear calcium solution is not evidence that calcium and sulfate were omitted from its dissolved inventory.

cases.title: Cross the silver-chloride ion-product threshold
cases.original_physical_forecast: The first trace additions are below the precipitation threshold; increasing both ion inventories crosses the solubility-product boundary.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: There is no substantial AgCl solid at the trace-loading snapshot.
The later snapshot contains AgCl solid while dissolved silver and chloride remain finite.

cases.title: Selectively dissolve carbonate from a mixed mineral precipitate
cases.original_physical_forecast: Acid removes calcium carbonate from a mixture containing barium sulfate, after which filtration retains the sulfate-rich residue.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Calcium transfers mainly to the filtrate, while barium remains mainly in retained sulfate solid.
Track gaseous carbon separately; the mass loss is not solely a filtration loss.

cases.title: One mixture can contain two distinct precipitates
cases.original_physical_forecast: Barium chloride supplies barium for sulfate precipitation and chloride for silver precipitation, yielding a mixed solid fraction.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Require phase-resolved evidence for both AgCl and BaSO4, not just an undifferentiated white solid.
The filtrate should retain spectator ions and any stoichiometric chloride excess.

cases.title: Iodide precipitation extends the silver-halide test
cases.original_physical_forecast: Chemical expectation: iodide and silver ions form poorly soluble silver iodide, commonly described as a yellow precipitate.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Require an identified silver-iodide solid or an explicit unsupported-phase outcome.
Do not count an AgCl-like generic precipitate or a successful command exit as confirmation.

cases.title: Bromide precipitation without inventing an unregistered salt bottle
cases.original_physical_forecast: Chemical expectation: bromide from hydrobromic acid forms a pale silver-bromide precipitate with silver ions.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Verify bromide and silver conservation and a specifically identified AgBr solid.
Missing AgBr phase support is recorded as unsupported, not as evidence that no real chemical reaction exists.

cases.title: Ferric ions oxidise copper without needing a noble-metal salt
cases.original_physical_forecast: Ferric ions can accept electrons from copper, producing ferrous and cupric ions rather than plating a second metal.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Check for Cu(II) generation accompanied by Fe(III)-to-Fe(II) reduction.
The ferric electron budget supports at most 0.001 mol copper oxidation before other oxidants are considered.

cases.title: Ferric ions oxidise iodide to iodine
cases.original_physical_forecast: Chemical expectation: ferric ions oxidise iodide while being reduced to ferrous ions, producing an iodine-containing pool.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Link any iodine production to an appropriate decrease in ferric and increase in ferrous inventory.
Distinguish I2 from triiodide complexation and from the original yellow ferric solution.

cases.title: Neutral permanganate and ethanol produce a different manganese endpoint
cases.original_physical_forecast: The documented non-acidified teaching route forms MnO2 and an acetic-acid/acetate product pool, rather than treating every permanganate reduction as Mn(II).

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: A manganese-dioxide solid should appear as permanganate declines.
Inspect the acid/base-adjusted organic product pool and total manganese; the displayed gross equation is followed by aqueous equilibration.

cases.title: A zinc concentration cell reverses sign when electrodes are swapped
cases.original_physical_forecast: The concentration difference generates a non-zero voltage, and reversing the electrode order reverses its sign without changing the chemistry.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: The two readings have approximately equal magnitudes and opposite signs.
Use zinc activity, not just nominal ZnSO4 molarity, for a Nernst comparison.

cases.title: Copper sulfate electrolysis competes with hydrogen evolution
cases.original_physical_forecast: With an inert-anode, copper-deposition interpretation, a small charge can reduce Cu(II) to copper while anodic water oxidation generates oxygen and acidity.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Require explicitly identified deposited copper and a charge-consistent Cu(II) decrease.
Check the model’s electrode assumptions and competing H2/O2 routes before comparing with the ideal equation.

cases.title: Warm water retains a smaller fraction of a finite CO2 dose
cases.original_physical_forecast: Warming normally favours CO2 release into the gas phase. Pressure also changes directly with temperature, so phase inventories are needed to separate the effects.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare dissolved-carbon fractions, not just the raw pressure difference.
Check whether the runtime uses temperature-dependent partition data; fixed-Henry behaviour is a model limitation.

cases.title: An inert gas at fixed volume changes total pressure, not the carbon dose
cases.original_physical_forecast: Adding inert gas to a fixed headspace increases total pressure without adding carbon. In an ideal mixture at fixed temperature, it does not directly multiply CO2 partial pressure.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Total pressure rises, but total carbon remains unchanged.
Compare CO2 partial pressure and dissolved-carbon fraction before and after; account for thermal and nonideal corrections.

cases.title: Stirring gives a bounded heterogeneous-catalyst rate enhancement
cases.original_physical_forecast: A vigorously stirred catalyst suspension is expected to consume peroxide faster than a minimally stirred one, without an unbounded proportional gain with rpm.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Inspect each vessel’s elapsed time before comparing peroxide conversion; unequal time advancement makes the comparison inconclusive.
At matched exposure, the vigorously stirred vessel should show greater conversion without catalyst consumption.

cases.title: Enzyme loading affects the early peroxide-decomposition rate
cases.original_physical_forecast: The higher catalase loading produces a larger early peroxide loss, before substrate exhaustion masks the dose response.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Compare fractional peroxide loss at the same very early virtual time.
Both enzyme inventories remain present; do not infer a universal real-world turnover rate from this model.

cases.title: Filtration distinguishes a soluble enzyme from a solid catalyst
cases.original_physical_forecast: An ideal filter retains solid MnO2 but passes molecularly represented catalase, so the two filtrates differ in catalytic activity.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Verify catalyst ownership after filtration before judging the reaction.
The catalase-containing filtrate consumes more peroxide than the MnO2-free filtrate at the same elapsed time.

cases.title: Equal time intervals consume progressively less substrate
cases.original_physical_forecast: With nearly constant catalytic conditions, a first-order-like substrate decay consumes less absolute peroxide in each successive equal interval.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Peroxide decreases monotonically and never becomes negative.
Compare consecutive mole losses, allowing a small thermal-rate change rather than assuming exactly isothermal decay.

cases.title: An iodine clock separates production from visible accumulation
cases.original_physical_forecast: Peroxide generates iodine while thiosulfate removes it. A larger scavenger inventory delays accumulation of an oxidised-iodine signal.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Evaluate I2/I3- inventory alongside remaining thiosulfate at each timepoint.
Require a later iodine-accumulation threshold in the larger-scavenger case, or report that the chosen sampling missed it.

cases.title: A sulfur clock can become acid-limited before all substrate is consumed
cases.original_physical_forecast: Limited acidity slows or arrests substantial conversion while thiosulfate remains; a fresh acid pulse restores the chemical driving conditions for further decomposition.

original_acceptance_checks.criterion: Residual thiosulfate coexists with a depleted acid reserve before the second acid addition.
